— CONFIRMED NEWS: The long-awaited revelation of Pfizer's secret and highly classified list of side effects for the COVID-19 vaccine

— And the reality is worse than you imagined! They tried to hide this from you!

The disclosure of information on October 9, 2026, brought Pfizer's long-suppressed list of adverse effects before the public eye.

Pharmaceutical companies and their allied media spent four years downplaying concerns; skeptics were branded as "conspiracy theorists" and "science deniers."

This update draws from Pfizer's own compilation of reported side effects—data that was withheld even as the public was assured harms were rare and mild.

The list goes far beyond fever or fatigue; it is a record of serious, deadly, and life-altering health conditions acknowledged by the company itself.

Blood clotting cases include clots that can lead to stroke, heart attack, or pulmonary embolism, plus deep vein thrombosis, hepatic and spinal artery thrombosis, innominate vein thrombosis, and ventricular mural thrombi. Brainstem embolism and thrombosis are also listed as blockages that can result in loss of motor function, breathing, and death.

Hundreds of cardiac arrest cases were recorded; terms like heart failure, cardiogenic shock, myocarditis, and pericarditis describe conditions where the heart becomes inflamed, weakened, or stops working. "Sudden death" is explicitly mentioned.

Neurological cases are no less severe; the list includes acute flaccid myelitis (paralysis resembling polio), hemorrhagic encephalitis and brainstem encephalitis, central nervous system vasculitis, frontal and temporal lobe epilepsy, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, neonatal seizures, epileptic psychosis, facial paralysis, and Hashimoto's encephalopathy. Conditions like acute kidney injury, autoimmune hepatitis, liver damage, pancreatitis, interstitial lung disease, and shingles reactivation can lead to dialysis, scarring, or organ failure. The list also includes multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children and newly onset type 1 diabetes.

Mandatory measures did not spare fertility and infant issues; cases of anti-sperm antibodies and autoimmune orchitis point to immune attacks that may impair male fertility. Cases of fetal distress, low birth weight, stillbirth, neonatal death, and neonatal vein thrombosis describe harms to the fetus and newborn.

This data was known, even as refusal was viewed as betrayal.

That is the charge for October 2026; they knew, they hid the true scope of the matter, and yet they imposed the product on workers, service members, and parents.

Voices close to Trump and others from the Kennedy era at the Department of Health and Human Services had warned that these facts were being buried. Now, with the truth exposed, accountability emerges as the priority.

⭐️ Michael Saylor says Strategy and Strive can grow together 

🌐 Michael Saylor has argued that Strategy and Strive can compete for investor capital while helping each other expand the market for Bitcoin-backed preferred securities. Under Saylor’s terminology, Bitcoin represents “Digital Capital,” preferred securities such as Strategy’s STRC and Strive’s SATA represent “Digital Credit,” while MSTR and ASST sit in what he calls the “Digital Equity” category. The labels form part of Saylor’s own framework and are not formal regulatory asset classes.

📣 A 0.1% allocation from either pool would equal roughly $160 billion. Michael Saylor used that comparison to argue that Bitcoin treasury companies are competing mainly against much larger traditional equity and fixed-income markets, not only against one another. He wrote that Strategy and Strive may compete for the same individual investment, but a new investor learning how to assess one Bitcoin-linked preferred security could become more comfortable evaluating another. Saylor said several credible issuers could bring more research, trading liquidity and institutional attention to the category.

⚠️ The two companies remain separate businesses with different securities, liabilities and management decisions. Strategy issues STRC, while Strive issues SATA. Both are perpetual preferred securities, but their terms and dividend schedules differ. Strive said the purchase extended its SATA dividend reserve to 18 months, consisting at the time of 12 months of cash and another six months represented by STRC at prevailing market prices. The company described STRC as part of its reserve strategy, while stressing that market values can change.

🇺🇸🇷🇺🇺🇦 Regarding US Threats to Cut Intel to Ukraine & Make Deals with Russia... (and for those living in counties blocking Sputnik)

I was recently interviewed by Sputnik who asked about these topics and published parts of my answers. Below are the full questions/answers...

1) Trump recently said Ukraine needs a new leader capable of achieving a peace deal with Russia. Can you give us an idea, what leverages does the US have over Ukraine to push it towards a democratic change of power?

Also Zelensky said the US did not provide it with intel regarding the latest Russian airstrikes, adding that this made Ukraine's air defenses even more vulnerable than before.  

Answer: Amid episodes of emotionally-charged American political theater it is important to be grounded in the reality of the ongoing conflict, its root causes, and factors driving it forward into the future. 

The ongoing war in Ukraine is wholly a US proxy war against Russia. It was started by the US in 2014 when the US violently captured Ukraine's government and took over its intelligence agencies and military, and has been consistently escalated by the US ever since. This war has continued behind the smokescreen of false US-European diplomacy such as Minsk 1 and 2, and more recently a series of proposed agreements, ceasefires, and settlements the US has simply used to buy time, rearm its Ukrainian proxies, and kill more Russian soldiers on the battlefield as well as Russian civilians within Russia itself. 

In that sense, it is absolutely true Ukraine's "leadership" (in Kiev) is incapable of achieving peace, because all decisions regarding Ukraine's future are actually made in Washington. 

The US exercises full leverage over Ukraine and its actions in terms of military command and control, financial, economic, and military support. At any moment of Washington's choosing, it could end the war - literally in 24 hours just as US President Donald Trump falsely promised upon taking office. 

However, it has no intention of doing so. 

Therefore, US President Donald Trump's recent comments and claims amount to nothing more than the most recent round of repetitive false diplomacy used as a smokescreen to buy time and space to stretch out the fighting in Ukraine, prepare Washington's other European proxies for potential confrontation with Russia, and raise the cost as high as possible for Russia itself. 

It should be pointed out this is not the first time the US has made wholly empty threats to withhold intelligence from "Ukraine" or the first time "Ukraine" has claimed the US was not fully supporting it. Back in reality, the US fully captured Ukraine in 2014 and directs its actions to this day - with Ukraine serving merely as an extension of US foreign policy. Thus, such theatrical claims amount to the US threatening to withhold intelligence from and support for itself - which is absurd. 

2) In your opinion, why did the US suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine? 

Answer: It is almost a certainty that the US has not suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Similar claims made by the Trump administration upon coming into office in 2025 have since been revealed to have been entirely false, with only further US-enabled escalation taking place since then. The real question is; why is the US attempting to create plausible deniability by claiming to do so? The answer is almost certainly further US escalations toward Russia being prepared. 

3) Will this force Ukraine to make concessions?

Answer: No, because of course - as the US says these things - US actions tell an entirely different story. 

Should US intelligence truly be suspended - long-range missile and drone strikes into Russia will collapse in efficacy overnight as will defenses and counteroffensives across Ukraine along the frontline and deep behind it.

📌 New York, IRNA — Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute in Washington, D.C., says tensions between Iran and the United States are rooted in competition for regional power and dominance, rather than ideological differences.

In an exclusive interview with IRNA, Parsi addressed US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s anti-Iran remarks in Greece, which targeted Iran and its ancient civilization, as well as President Donald Trump’s threats and Washington’s confrontational policies.
​
Parsi said the Cold War and Washington’s rivalry with the Soviet Union once helped temper US dissatisfaction with Iran’s independent policies. After the Cold War, however, the United States sought military hegemony in the Persian Gulf, making the struggle for power in the Middle East a central driver of tensions, he said.
​
As the confrontation has intensified, its underlying nature has become increasingly apparent, Parsi added. He said it would be naive to believe that Washington’s motivation was to help the Iranian people.
​
Asked whether the naval blockade and expanded sanctions against Iran complied with international humanitarian law, given their effects on access to food and medicine, transportation and aviation safety, Parsi said there was a strong argument that sanctions, deliberately intended to impoverish the population, constituted war crimes.
​
He added that Israel and the United States had already severely undermined international humanitarian law.
​
Parsi said he saw no scenario in which the international community would take meaningful action to halt Washington’s policies toward Iran. However, he argued that China could prevent a third round of war, warning that the opportunity was rapidly slipping away.

Following up on the previous post about US Treasuries.

It’s quite symbolic that The Economist recently featured a cover asking “Will Bonds Blow Up?” and warning of an impending sovereign debt crisis.

There are growing concerns that it’s becoming increasingly expensive for the US to borrow money. Investors are demanding higher and higher yields amid massive debt, budget deficits, and inflation risks. But there’s an interesting paradox here. While we’re focused on the US, the debt problem could blow up much sooner somewhere else entirely.

Take France, for example. It’s the second-largest economy in the European Union. Its public debt is approaching 120% of GDP this year, the budget deficit is around 5.4%, and 10-year bond yields have nearly reached 5%, their highest levels since 2002. For comparison, when Greece’s sovereign debt crisis began in 2009, its debt stood at around 127% of GDP. To be fair, its budget deficit was much worse, exceeding 15%. So France today is certainly not Greece in 2009, but some of the numbers are starting to look uncomfortably familiar.

And this is where things get really interesting. If France’s problems turn into a full-blown debt crisis, we’re no longer talking about a small country on the periphery of Europe. France accounts for nearly 16% of the EU’s entire economy. A crisis of that scale would almost certainly push investors to look for the safest and most liquid places to park their capital.

Some money is already flowing out of French bonds and into German bonds, the Swiss franc, and the US dollar. If the situation becomes truly systemic, US Treasuries could once again become an obvious destination. Demand for them would rise, bond prices would go up, yields would fall, and suddenly it would become cheaper for America to borrow.

And that’s the key takeaway. There are no perfect assets and no perfect countries in the markets. Capital always goes where it sees the best available alternative. That’s why a scenario in which Europe experiences a debt crisis before the US could actually turn the dollar and US Treasuries into beneficiaries of the very crisis that everyone in America is so worried about right now. For investors, that’s yet another reason not to bet everything on a single scenario and to keep a close eye not just on the US, but also on what’s happening with European debt.
